questions.question: For closed subsets $(\boldsymbol{E}_i)_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ of a metric space, what does the proposition say about $\bigcap_{i = 1}^{\infty}\boldsymbol{E}_i$?
options: It is always open but not closed.
It is closed only when the sets are finite.

questions.question: For closed subsets $\boldsymbol{E}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{E}_k$, what does the proposition say about $\bigcup_{i = 1}^{k}\boldsymbol{E}_i$?
options: It is open but not closed.

questions.question: In a metric space $\boldsymbol{X}$, which of the following is always closed?
In $\mathbb{R}$, what is $\bigcap_{n = 1}^{\infty}[-\frac{1}{n},\frac{1}{n}]$?
Which operation on closed sets is guaranteed to preserve closedness only in the finite case in the proposition?
Which stronger statement is true for closed sets?
options: Any union of closed sets is closed, even for uncountable families.
Only countable intersections of closed sets are closed.
Closed sets are preserved only under pairwise intersections.
Any intersection of closed sets is closed, even for uncountable families.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$, what does the $\bigcup_{n = 1}^{\infty}[0,1-\frac{1}{n}]$ show?
options: A finite union of closed sets can fail to be closed.
A countable intersection of closed sets can fail to be closed.
An infinite union of closed sets can fail to be closed.

questions.question: If $\boldsymbol{E}_1,\boldsymbol{E}_2,\boldsymbol{E}_3$ are closed subsets of a metric space, what can be concluded about $\boldsymbol{E}_1\cup\boldsymbol{E}_2\cup\boldsymbol{E}_3$?
options: It is not closed unless the sets are disjoint.
It is open but not closed.

questions.question: Which word cannot be dropped from the statement that unions of closed sets are closed?
Why is the statement about intersections of closed sets stronger than merely countable intersections?
options: It only works for two closed sets.
It requires every closed set to be bounded, for every possible choice of input.
It remains true for arbitrary, even uncountable, families.
It says that every union is also closed.

questions.question: A student claims that $\bigcup_{n = 1}^{\infty}[0,1-\frac{1}{n}]$ is closed because every set in the union is closed. What is the error?
options: The theorem only guarantees finite unions of closed sets.
Closedness is never preserved by unions, in all instances without exception.

questions.question: Let $(\boldsymbol{F}_\alpha)_{\alpha\in A}$ be an arbitrary family of closed subsets of a metric space. What can be concluded about $\bigcap_{\alpha\in A}\boldsymbol{F}_\alpha$?
options: It is closed only if $A$ is countable.
It is open but not closed.
It is closed only if every $\boldsymbol{F}_\alpha$ is non-empty.

questions.question: Which operation preserves closedness for any family of closed sets?
Which union of closed sets is guaranteed to be closed?
options: Only a countable union of open sets

questions.question: Which two sets are always closed in a metric space?
If $E_1$ and $E_2$ are closed, what can be concluded about $E_1\cup E_2$?
options: It is always open but not closed.

questions.question: If $(E_i)_{i=1}^{\infty}$ are closed, what can be concluded about $\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty}E_i$?
options: It must be open but not closed.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$, what is $\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}[-1/n,1/n]$?
Why is the word finite important for unions of closed sets?
options: Finite unions of closed sets may fail to be closed.
The whole space is not closed.
Infinite unions of closed sets may fail to be closed.

questions.question: Which set is an infinite union of closed sets that is not closed in $\mathbb{R}$?
